findings.original: Have I tonight fluster’d with flowing cups,
findings.current: I've got tipsy tonight with overflowing cups,
findings.issue: The three Cypriots (lines 7-9) are the object of "fluster'd"; "I've got tipsy" reads as Iago himself getting drunk, which reverses the sense.
findings.proposed: I've made tipsy tonight with overflowing cups,

findings.current: Oh, so that's where the tail hangs — by the wind.
findings.issue: The tale/tail pun on the proverb "thereby hangs a tale" is lost; only the tail sense remains, so the musician's reply ("What tale...") makes no sense and the modern line is confusing.
findings.proposed: Oh, thereby hangs a tale — or a tail.

findings.original: More than their own! What then? How then?
findings.current: other than their own! What then? How then?
findings.issue: "their own" refers to eyes (no mortal eyes but their own will see them in bed), but with "share a pillow" on the line before it now reads as "a pillow other than their own".
findings.proposed: except their own eyes! What then? How then?

findings.original: I am not bound to that all slaves are free to.
findings.current: I'm not bound to what even slaves are free from.
findings.issue: The rendering keeps the knotty bound/free phrasing, so a modern reader won't see the point: even slaves aren't required to reveal their thoughts.
findings.proposed: I'm not bound to do what even slaves are free to refuse.

findings.original: That liv’st to make thine honesty a vice!
findings.current: who's lived to see his honesty turned into a vice!
findings.issue: Iago's self-address says he himself has made his honesty a vice; the rendering shifts to a passive "see it turned" and to third person, which weakens the self-reproach.
findings.proposed: you've lived to make your honesty a vice!

findings.original: Marry, sir, by many a wind instrument that I know. But, masters, here’s money for you: and the general so likes your music, that he desires you, for love’s sake, to make no more noise with it.
findings.current: Why, sir, a tail hangs by many a wind instrument I know — by many a farting backside. But, musicians, here's money for you: and the general likes your music so much that he asks you, for love's sake, to make no more noise with it.
findings.issue: The fart joke is only implied in the original; "farting backside" says it outright and is a bit coarser than needed, though it does make the joke readable.
findings.proposed: Why, sir, by many a wind instrument I know — the kind that blows from behind. But, musicians, here's money for you: and the general likes your music so much that he asks you, for love's sake, to make no more noise with it.
